description.narrative: E.1 Knowledge management and Communication The BioResilience approach to Knowledge Management and Communication will be designed and coordinated under component 4 although implementation will be done under the other project components. The strategy is thus necessarily inclusive of all the technical and policy topics covered by the project, consistently with the ultimate goal of promoting the incorporation of the also cross-cutting issues of land use and management, biodiversity and resilience to climate change into policy-making for human and socio-economic development. The specific related products are a communication strategy and action plan, aimed at raising awareness and mostly dedicated to local and national audiences; and a multiscale knowledge management strategy and action plan that includes the regional and global levels and the interaction with the BGI Global Platform. The project will develop an evidence-based approach to knowledge management that showcases the effectiveness and benefits of incorporating NCA, resilience building, and biodiversity protection within enhanced private sector investment towards nature-positive development. The interim and final results of the activities under the project, including lessons learned and best practices will be systematically identified, documented, and shared nationally and to the BGI Global Knowledge Management and Learning mechanism for the benefit of participating countries. This includes reporting to and benefitting from the “Solutions Portal” that will facilitate sharing and scaling NbS, as well as contributing to other global databases, such as World Overview of Conservation Approaches and Technologies (WOCAT), and regional Knowledge Management platforms such as the SOILCARE Caribbean LDN and SLM Knowledge Hub and the SIDS-SIDS Green-Blue Economy Knowledge Transfer Hub. It is also planned the participation in the BGI Global Coordination Project annual meetings, Regional Nodes and Thematic Working Groups, for sharing and learning for effective upscaling and replication of successful solutions. In order to learn and share experiences with other ongoing and upcoming projects in the country, the BioResilience knowledge sharing strategy will also consider links with the NZNP Accelerator Platform, part of the GEF-8 NZNP Integrated Programme (IP), and with the global multi-stakeholder platform that will be developed under the CHO-IP, as T&T makes part of both GEF-8 initiatives. The BioResilience communication strategy will be gender and age-sensitive, to guide messaging to appropriate audiences using diverse communication channels to disseminate project approaches and findings, share best practices, and showcasing the full potential of NbS for environmental and socio-economic wellbeing. Public awareness will be a cross-cutting theme to ensure that communities are engaged and consulted and are active participants in the full project's implementation cycle. This is particularly critical for increasing farmer’s engagement in component 2 activities (RECSOIL), so specific actions will be implemented to that end. Collaborations will be ensured with the GoRTT, UWI and CBOs that work in the project area, so project results can be communicated and integrated with local knowledge at the site level. Local-level actors will be sensitized of all activities and the link between biodiversity and livelihoods will be highlighted to enhance the adoption of initiatives. This is critical so that the learning gleaned through the project can be disseminated in relevant ways to stakeholders. An overall budget for communication and knowledge management of $150,750 is allocated as follows, with the timeline of activities as per the workplan in Annex D: Activity Unit No of units Unit cost USD Total USD Communications Specialist Day 100 300 30,000 Gender Specialist Day 150 250 37,500 M&E Specialist – partially cofinanced Day 25 300 7,500 Terminal workshop Lumpsum 1 7,000 7,000 Inception workshop Lumpsum 1 1,000 1,000 In-Country meetings/focus group discussions/workshops Lumpsum 2 5,000 10,000 Publications (Dissemination of findings) Lumpsum 2 6,375 12,750 BGI IP global Platform meetings + regional meetings Trip 9 5,000 45,000 Total 150,750 E.2 Socio-economic Benefits and Decent Rural Employment[37] The specific socioeconomic benefits of the project at the national and local levels include: · Improved national capacity to account for changes in natural capital in the AFOLU sectors for better management of natural resources that contribute to sustainable economic development (Component 1); · Improved capacity (awareness, attitude, knowledge, skills and incentives) of local smallholder farmers to be good stewards of agricultural soils (Component 3); · Increased climate resilience of smallholder farming livelihoods from the adoption of SSM practices that increase SOC (Component 2); · Improved national food and nutrition security due to enhanced quality of crops grown in healthier more productive soils (Component 2). · Empowerment of women and young agropreneurs to create or scale-up sustainable nature-positive business entreprises (Component 3); · Increased income earning opportunities for rural communities operating eco-tourism enterprises around PAs due to increased marketing of natural assets of PAs (Component 3); · Mobilisation of new finance sources, including from private sector, to support adoption of NbS and investment in nature-positive business enterprises (Component 3); · Short term income earning opportunities created for community reforestation groups providing skilled labour for riverside revegetation activities (Component 2); · Reduced disaster risk of rural communities from flooding and drought due to improved watershed restoration (Component 3); · Enhanced social and economic impact of future projects and initiatives through the documentation and dissemination of lessons learned and best practices that can be used for replication and up-scaling in other communities and SIDS (Component 4). [37] Specific guidance on how FAO can promote the Four Pillars of Decent Work in rural areas is provided in the Quick reference for addressing decent rural employment (as well as in the full corresponding Guidance document). For more information on FAO’s work on decent rural employment and related guidance materials please consult the FAO thematic website at: http://www.fao.org/rural-employment/en/.
Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

To halt current land degradation trends, increase biodiversity and provide resilience to climate change impacts for a nature-positive development, including sustainable tourism and increased food security in TT
